catalog_quote: G. Papuma. Although this language is spoken only in the village of Papuma, and not even in the whole of that, because it also houses a number of Ansus speakers, the Papuma speakers nevertheless number more than 700. Some of its grammatical details will be discussed later, but there is one feature that I wish to mention here: in Papuma word accent is distinctive, that is to say, there are words which may be distinguished by the place of the accent. For example: wéa — you stand, as opposed to weá — root. ... [p. 14, on the comparative wordlists:] Stress-accent, vowel pitch and vowel length (part of the accentual system in many of these languages) are not indicated.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (stress) is lexically contrastive in Papuma: the position of the accent is not predictable and distinguishes otherwise identical words (wéa 'you stand' vs weá 'root'). Anceaux gives no default position. Silzer 1983: 236-237 independently shows that Papuma verb stems, like Ambai's, fall into two lexical classes, stem-initial syllable stressed (t-u-anang 'you plant') vs unstressed (matai > motai 'you fear'), which is consistent with lexically specified stress rather than a positional rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement rests on one minimal pair from a 'short word-list' collected by Anceaux. The comparative wordlist deliberately omits accent marks (p. 14).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated words from a wordlist). Silzer's remarks concern inflected verb forms (subject-marked stems). No phrase-level or citation-form information.
new_statements.identity_note: Anceaux 1961 sec. G describes the language of Papuma village on Yapen (c. 700 speakers, village shared with Ansus speakers), which is exactly Glottolog papu1251 / ISO ppm; no dialects are named. Silzer 1983's 'Papuma' data (Appendix A, pp. 235-238, and pp. 155-156) refer to the same language.
